title: Identification of cross-reactive microbiota against the prefusion F protein
summary:
Background:
Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) is a major cause of respiratory infections that can lead to severe illnesses such as bronchiolitis, particularly in infants and individuals with weakened immune systems. Recently, an RSV vaccine has become available for older adults and people at high risk.

In addition to the immune system, the so-called microbiome—the community of bacteria living in and on our bodies—plays an important role in our health. The microbiome of the respiratory tract can influence both the severity of RSV infections and the effectiveness of vaccines. Some bacteria can train the immune system or even bind antibodies that are originally directed against viruses. These “cross-reactive” effects may enhance or weaken the protection provided by vaccination.

Aim of the Study:
We aim to investigate whether specific bacteria in the saliva of patients influence the immune response after RSV vaccination. In particular, we are interested in whether certain bacteria can bind antibodies against the prefusion F protein of RSV and whether the presence of these bacteria is associated with antibody levels in the blood and saliva or with the T-cell response after vaccination.
conditions: Respiratory syncytial virus as the cause of diseases classified to other chapters

interventions.name: In this study, saliva and blood samples will be collected from all enrolled participants at three time points during routine blood draws in the outpatient clinic: immediately before RSV vaccination (day 0), approximately one month after vaccination (month 1), and approximately 3–6 months after vacci

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
all patients who are vaccinated as part of routine care
Exclusion criteria:
-Inability to fully comprehend the informed consent, and minors.
-Known infection with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), presence of active -hepatitis C or active hepatitis B infection, as well as any uncontrolled active systemic infection.
-Any concurrent medical or psychological condition that may impair the ability to provide consent.
-Individuals detained by a public authority under legal mandate.
-Lack of willingness to consent to the storage of pseudonymized medical data related to the study.
-Lack of willingness to permit the collection of study-relevant personal data.
